subject: Medicine
topic: High-Risk Solitary Pulmonary Nodule: Tissue Biopsy vs Surveillance
stem: A 64-year-old man presents to the clinic for evaluation of an incidental chest finding. He was seen in the emergency department 1 week ago following a minor motor vehicle collision, where a non-contrast trauma chest CT revealed a solitary 1.8-cm non-calcified, spiculated nodule in the right upper pulmonary lobe. He has no cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnea, fever, or weight loss. His past medical history is significant for coronary artery disease and hypertension. He has a 42-pack-year cigarette smoking history and continues to smoke 1 pack daily. Physical examination reveals clear lung fields bilaterally and no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. Previous chest radiographs from 5 years ago are retrieved and show clear lung fields with no visible nodules. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the clinical management of this patient's pulmonary nodule?

options.text: Schedule low-dose serial non-contrast chest CT surveillance in 6 to 12 months to assess for volumetric growth
options.explanation: Watchful waiting with follow-up CT is appropriate only for low-risk, small nodules (< 6-8 mm) or non-smokers; a 1.8-cm spiculated upper-lobe nodule in a heavy smoker requires immediate tissue evaluation.

options.text: Prescribe a 14-day course of oral levofloxacin and repeat chest radiography in 6 weeks to rule out infectious infiltrate
options.explanation: Empiric antibiotics for an asymptomatic, non-calcified spiculated nodule in a heavy smoker is an outdated, dangerous practice that delays lung cancer diagnosis.

options.text: Perform 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET/CT) or obtain tissue biopsy / surgical wedge resection
options.explanation: This patient presents with a solitary pulmonary nodule (SPN; discrete parenchymal opacity <= 3 cm surrounded by normal lung). Management of an SPN is determined by assessing the pretest probability of malignancy based on patient and radiographic characteristics: (1) High-risk patient characteristics: older age (> 60 years), heavy smoking history (42 pack-years), family history of lung cancer, and occupational asbestos exposure. (2) High-risk radiographic features: size > 8 mm (here 1.8 cm / 18 mm), spiculated or corona radiata borders, upper lobe location, ground-glass or subsolid attenuation, absence of benign calcification (e.g., popcorn, concentric, diffuse), and absence of stability on prior imaging over 2 years. Based on Fleischner Society and ACCP guidelines, a nodule with high pretest probability of malignancy (> 65% risk) requires definitive tissue diagnosis: either 18F-FDG PET/CT scan to assess metabolic activity and mediastinal staging, followed by percutaneous transthoracic needle biopsy, bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS), or direct video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) excisional wedge resection. Serial CT surveillance at 3–6 months is strictly contraindicated in high-risk nodules > 8 mm, as it delays curable early-stage lung cancer resection.

options.text: Perform sputum cytology and expectorant acid-fast bacillus cultures
options.explanation: Sputum cytology has extremely low sensitivity (< 20–30%) for peripheral solitary pulmonary nodules and should not replace tissue biopsy or PET-CT.

options.text: Reassure the patient that the nodule is benign because he has no respiratory symptoms or hemoptysis
options.explanation: Early-stage resectable lung cancers are completely asymptomatic; relying on symptoms to suspect malignancy results in metastatic presentation.

explanation: A solitary pulmonary nodule > 8 mm with high-risk features (spiculated margins, upper lobe location, older age, heavy smoking history) has a high probability of malignancy. According to Fleischner Society guidelines, high-risk nodules mandate 18F-FDG PET/CT and/or tissue biopsy / surgical excision (VATS wedge resection). Serial CT surveillance is inappropriate for high-risk nodules > 8 mm, and empiric antibiotics cause dangerous diagnostic delay.
objective: Select PET-CT or tissue biopsy/resection for high-risk solitary pulmonary nodules (> 8 mm, spiculated borders, smoker) rather than low-risk surveillance.
keyPoints: Solitary pulmonary nodule > 8 mm with spiculated borders in a smoker = high pretest malignancy risk.
High-risk nodules mandate FDG-PET/CT, tissue biopsy, or surgical resection (VATS).
Do not perform serial CT surveillance or give empiric antibiotics for high-risk nodules.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Preoperative Fluid & Electrolyte Resuscitation
stem: A 4-week-old first-born male infant is brought to the pediatric emergency department by his mother due to progressively forceful, non-bilious vomiting after every feeding over the past 5 days. The mother states that he is constantly ravenous and vigorously latches onto the bottle immediately after vomiting. Birth and maternal prenatal history were uncomplicated. On physical examination, the infant appears lethargic with sunken anterior fontanelle, dry oral mucous membranes, and decreased skin turgor. A firm, mobile, non-tender, 1.5-cm olive-shaped mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant just lateral to the rectus abdominis. Abdominal ultrasonography confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with a pyloric muscle thickness of 4.5 mm (normal: < 3 mm) and channel length of 18 mm (normal: < 14 mm). Serum chemistry demonstrates: sodium 131 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, chloride 84 mEq/L, bicarbonate 34 mEq/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas reveals pH 7.52 and pCO2 44 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the clinical management of this infant?

options.text: Transfer the infant immediately to the operating room for emergency Ramstedt pyloromyotomy within 2 hours of arrival
options.explanation: Pyloromyotomy is not a surgical emergency; operating on an infant with severe metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia induces life-threatening anesthetic apnea and cardiac arrhythmias.

options.text: Place a nasogastric tube and perform emergent upper gastrointestinal barium fluoroscopy to rule out malrotation
options.explanation: Ultrasound has already confirmed hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; barium fluoroscopy is redundant, exposes the infant to radiation, and risks barium aspiration.

options.text: Administer oral atropine sulfate drops to relax the hypertrophied pyloric circular smooth muscle
options.explanation: Endoscopic balloon dilation or medical atropine is inferior, slow, and reserved only when surgery is strictly contraindicated.

options.text: Initiate intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid followed by 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline with potassium chloride until serum electrolytes and bicarbonate normalize, then perform pyloromyotomy
options.explanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is characterized by hypertrophy of the pyloric circular smooth muscle, causing gastric outlet obstruction. Classic features include non-bilious projectile vomiting in a hungry infant aged 3–6 weeks and a palpable "olive" mass. Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and water leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with secondary volume depletion. In response to hypovolemia, aldosterone acts on renal collecting ducts to reabsorb sodium in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, resulting in severe potassium depletion and paradoxical aciduria. The single most important surgical principle in IHPS is that pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt pyloromyotomy) is NEVER a surgical emergency—it is a MEDICAL emergency requiring complete electrolyte and acid-base resuscitation PRIOR to surgery. Administering general anesthesia to an alkalotic, hypokalemic infant causes fatal postoperative hypoventilation and central apnea (alkalosis blunts central chemoreceptor respiratory drive). Fluid management begins with an isotonic saline bolus (20 mL/kg) for shock, followed by maintenance fluid with 5% dextrose in 0.45% saline plus potassium chloride (20–40 mEq/L) once urine output is verified, until serum chloride > 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate < 28 mEq/L, and potassium > 4.0 mEq/L.

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct paradoxical aciduria
options.explanation: The infant has severe systemic metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, bicarbonate 34); administering sodium bicarbonate is lethal.

explanation: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from persistent vomiting of gastric HCl. Pyloromyotomy is a medical, not surgical, emergency: surgery must be DEFERRED until dehydration and electrolyte derangements are fully corrected with IV fluids and potassium. Anesthesia during uncorrected metabolic alkalosis carries high risk of central apnea and cardiac arrest.
objective: Prioritize intravenous fluid and electrolyte correction over immediate surgery in infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis to prevent postoperative anesthetic apnea.
keyPoints: Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
Pyloromyotomy is NOT an emergency; surgical correction is performed only AFTER electrolytes normalize.
Operating on an uncorrected alkalotic infant risks catastrophic postoperative respiratory depression/apnea.

subject: Neurology
topic: Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Serial Respiratory Parameter Monitoring & Immunotherapy
stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of progressive tingling in his toes and fingers followed by symmetrical weakness in both lower extremities that has now progressed to involve his arms. Two weeks ago, he had a self-limited diarrheal illness after a barbecue. Vital signs are: blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Neurological examination reveals bilateral, symmetrical lower motor neuron weakness (muscle strength 3/5 in lower extremities, 4/5 in upper extremities), absent deep tendon reflexes (patellar, Achilles, and biceps 0/4), and mild stocking-glove vibratory sensation loss. Lumbar puncture demonstrates: opening pressure 140 mm H2O, protein 168 mg/dL (reference: 15–45 mg/dL), leukocytes 2/mcL (albuminocytologic dissociation), and normal glucose. Which of the following is the most critical immediate step in the ongoing clinical management of this patient?

options.text: Initiate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 5 days to reduce nerve root inflammation
options.explanation: Multiple randomized controlled trials have proven that systemic corticosteroids (IV or oral) are completely ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and may actually delay recovery.

options.text: Rely on continuous pulse oximetry and initiate arterial blood gas testing only if oxygen saturation drops below 92%
options.explanation: Pulse oximetry is a late and dangerous indicator of neuromuscular respiratory failure; mechanics fail and CO2 retention occurs long before hypoxia develops.

options.text: Administer intravenous pyridostigmine to enhance acetylcholine transmission at the neuromuscular junction
options.explanation: Pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for myasthenia gravis; it has zero efficacy in autoimmune peripheral demyelinating neuropathy and increases airway secretions.

options.text: Administer oral ciprofloxacin to eradicate persistent gastrointestinal Campylobacter colonisation
options.explanation: GBS is a post-infectious autoimmune phenomenon occurring weeks after the enteric infection has resolved; antibiotics do not alter the neurological course.

options.text: Perform serial bedside spirometry measuring forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF), and initiate intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange
options.explanation: This patient presents with Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS; acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy [AIDP]), most commonly triggered by molecular mimicry following Campylobacter jejuni enteritis (anti-GM1/GD1a ganglioside antibodies). Hallmarks are symmetric ascending flaccid quadriparesis, hyporeflexia/areflexia, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count). The single greatest life-threatening complication of GBS is acute neuromuscular respiratory failure due to diaphragm and intercostal muscle paralysis, occurring in up to 30% of patients. Crucially, pulse oximetry and arterial blood gases remain deceptively normal until catastrophic sudden respiratory arrest occurs. Therefore, the single most critical management priority is SERIAL bedside monitoring of respiratory mechanics: (1) Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) and (2) Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF, or maximal inspiratory pressure). Indications for preemptive ICU admission and elective endotracheal intubation include: FVC < 15–20 mL/kg (or > 30% drop), NIF worse than -30 cm H2O (i.e., -20 to 0 cm H2O), or vital capacity < 1 liter. Disease-modifying therapy is IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) OR plasmapheresis (plasma exchange); both have equivalent efficacy. Corticosteroids are completely INEFFECTIVE and not recommended.

explanation: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (ascending weakness, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation) carries a 30% risk of acute neuromuscular respiratory failure. Monitoring requires SERIAL measurements of forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force (NIF), as pulse oximetry remains normal until terminal arrest. First-line disease-modifying treatment is IVIG or plasmapheresis. Corticosteroids are ineffective in GBS.
objective: Prioritize serial pulmonary mechanics monitoring (FVC and NIF) and immunotherapy (IVIG or plasmapheresis) in Guillain-Barré syndrome while recognizing corticosteroids are ineffective.
keyPoints: GBS triad: ascending weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation.
Monitor respiratory mechanics with serial FVC and NIF; pulse oximetry drops too late.
First-line immunotherapy: IVIG or plasmapheresis (equivalent efficacy); corticosteroids are ineffective.

subject: Obstetrics
topic: Fetal Growth Restriction & Umbilical Artery Doppler Absent End-Diastolic Flow
stem: A 31-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks gestation presents for a scheduled maternal-fetal medicine follow-up ultrasound. She has chronic hypertension controlled on oral labetalol. Routine anatomical survey at 20 weeks was normal. Today, serial biometric ultrasonography reveals severe fetal growth restriction (FGR): estimated fetal weight is at the 2nd percentile for gestational age, and amniotic fluid index is 3.4 cm (oligohydramnios). Umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry demonstrates persistent absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF). Fetal cardiotocography demonstrates a reactive nonstress test with a baseline heart rate of 145/min, moderate variability, and two 15-beat accelerations lasting 15 seconds. Maternal blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg, and she has no proteinuria, headache, or visual changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Administer intramuscular antenatal betamethasone, admit for continuous inpatient fetal surveillance, and deliver at 33 to 34 weeks (or sooner if testing deteriorates)
options.explanation: Fetal growth restriction (FGR; estimated fetal weight < 10th percentile) is most commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency. When placental vascular resistance rises due to obliteration of tertiary stem villi, blood flow through the umbilical artery in diastole progressively diminishes, progressing from decreased end-diastolic flow -> Absent End-Diastolic Flow (AEDF) -> Reversed End-Diastolic Flow (REDF). Umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry is the primary surveillance tool that guides delivery timing: (1) Absent end-diastolic velocity reflects >= 70% obliteration of the placental microvasculature, placing the fetus at extreme risk of intrauterine acidosis and stillbirth. (2) According to SMFM and ACOG guidelines, persistent AEDF at or beyond 32 0/7 weeks gestation is an indication for: (a) Hospital admission and close inpatient surveillance (daily nonstress testing / biophysical profiles), (b) Administration of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) to accelerate fetal lung maturation, and (c) Delivery at 33 0/7 to 34 0/7 weeks gestation (or immediately if reversed end-diastolic flow [REDF] develops, if the biophysical profile is <= 4/10, or if nonreassuring testing occurs). (3) Expectant outpatient management to 37–39 weeks in the presence of AEDF carries an unacceptable risk of fetal demise.

options.text: Reassure the patient based on the reactive nonstress test and schedule repeat outpatient ultrasound in 4 weeks
options.explanation: A reactive NST reflects current status but does not mitigate the extreme risk of sudden fetal death in placental failure with AEDF; outpatient 4-week follow-up is negligent.

options.text: Perform emergent cesarean delivery under general anesthesia within 1 hour without corticosteroid administration
options.explanation: In the presence of a reactive NST and absent maternal acute instability, there is time to administer antenatal betamethasone to reduce neonatal RDS, IVH, and mortality prior to delivery.

options.text: Increase maternal oral labetalol dosage to lower systolic blood pressure to < 110 mmHg to enhance placental perfusion
options.explanation: Aggressive blood pressure reduction decreases uterine artery perfusion pressure, further starving the ischemic placenta and precipitating acute fetal bradycardia.

options.text: Initiate maternal intravenous heparin anticoagulation to dissolve placental villous microthrombi
options.explanation: Heparin does not reverse established placental vascular obliteration in FGR and exposes the mother to hemorrhage during delivery.

explanation: Fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight < 10th percentile) complicated by umbilical artery Doppler absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) indicates severe placental vascular resistance. SMFM/ACOG guidelines mandate: (1) Inpatient admission with intensive surveillance, (2) Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) for lung maturity, and (3) Delivery at 33–34 weeks (or emergent delivery if reversed end-diastolic flow or nonreassuring testing occurs).
objective: Manage fetal growth restriction with absent end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler: antenatal corticosteroids, inpatient surveillance, and delivery at 33–34 weeks.
keyPoints: Umbilical artery Doppler reflects placental resistance: normal -> decreased -> absent (AEDF) -> reversed (REDF).
Persistent AEDF indicates >= 70% placental obliteration: admit, administer betamethasone, and deliver at 33–34 weeks.
Reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) warrants immediate delivery at >= 30–32 weeks.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Delirium Diagnosis & Multicomponent Non-Pharmacological Management Strategy
stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the medical surgical unit for treatment of acute pyelonephritis with intravenous ceftriaxone. On hospital day 2 at 11:00 PM, the night nurse calls the physician because the patient is highly agitated, pulling at her peripheral intravenous line and Foley catheter, and attempting to climb out of bed. Her daughter states that before hospitalization the patient lived independently, managed her own finances, and had no memory deficits. On examination, the patient is disoriented to place and time, incorrectly insisting that she is in an airport. Her attention is markedly impaired; she cannot count backward from 20 to 1 or name the months of the year in reverse. Over a 30-minute interview, her consciousness waxes and wanes from combative agitation to profound lethargy. Physical examination reveals suprapubic tenderness and bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. Vital signs are: temperature 38.2 C (100.8 F), blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, heart rate 94/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on ambient air. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient's acute cognitive impairment?

options.text: Administer intravenous haloperidol 5 mg immediately and repeat every 4 hours around the clock to resolve delirium
options.explanation: Routine administration of antipsychotics does not prevent or resolve delirium, increases mortality in elderly patients, and causes extrapyramidal symptoms and QT prolongation.

options.text: Implement multicomponent non-pharmacological delirium interventions (frequent reorientation, lighting adjustments, family presence, early catheter removal) while identifying and treating underlying medical triggers
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute delirium (specifically mixed hyperactive/hypoactive delirium), characterized by an acute onset (hours to days), fluctuating course, impaired attention and awareness, and altered sleep-wake cycle. The acute onset, fluctuating cognitive state, and prominent inattention decisively differentiate delirium from major neurocognitive disorder (dementia), which has an insidious, progressive course with intact attention in early to moderate stages. Delirium in hospitalized elderly patients is almost always multifactorial, triggered by an acute medical illness (pyelonephritis/urosepsis), physical restraints, indwelling urinary catheters, unfamiliar environment, and sleep disruption. American Geriatrics Society (AGS) guidelines establish that the foundational, first-line management is NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL multicomponent interventions: (1) Reorientation strategies (clocks, calendars, verbal reorientation by staff and familiar family members), (2) Optimizing sensory input (ensuring patient has glasses and hearing aids), (3) Sleep hygiene (maintaining day/night circadian lighting, quiet environment at night, minimizing nocturnal vitals/blood draws), (4) Early removal of tethering lines (Foley catheters and unnecessary IV lines), and (5) Mobilization. Antipsychotics (such as haloperidol or quetiapine) carry black-box warnings and do NOT shorten delirium duration or improve mortality; they are reserved strictly as a last resort for severe, refractory agitation that poses an immediate danger to patient or staff safety.

options.text: Apply bilateral wrist restraints and vest restraints to the bed to prevent catheter dislodgement and falls
options.explanation: Physical restraints exacerbate agitation, increase fall-related head injuries, worsen delirium severity, and should be avoided.

options.text: Initiate oral donepezil 5 mg daily for rapid improvement of cognitive decline
options.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors treat chronic Alzheimer dementia; they have no role in acute delirium and worsen confusion and gastrointestinal symptoms.

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg for rapid sedation
options.explanation: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium, prolong hospital stay, and paradoxically increase agitation and fall risk (unless delirium is caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal).

explanation: Delirium is characterized by acute onset, fluctuating course, and marked inattention, distinguishing it from dementia. First-line management is non-pharmacological multicomponent environmental interventions (reorientation, sensory aids, sleep hygiene, family presence, removing tethers like Foley catheters) while treating the underlying medical cause (pyelonephritis). Antipsychotics are reserved solely for extreme violence/safety risk. Benzodiazepines and physical restraints worsen delirium.
objective: Distinguish delirium from dementia by acute onset and inattention, and apply first-line non-pharmacological multicomponent delirium interventions.
keyPoints: Delirium features: acute onset, fluctuating consciousness, and prominent inattention.
First-line management: treat underlying cause and apply non-pharmacological multicomponent interventions.
Antipsychotics do not cure delirium; physical restraints and benzodiazepines worsen delirium.

subject: Surgery
topic: Acute Testicular Torsion: Emergent Surgical Exploration & Bilateral Orchiopexy
stem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his father due to sudden-onset, severe, excruciating left scrotal and lower abdominal pain that awakened him from sleep 2 hours ago. He has had two episodes of non-bilious vomiting since the pain began. He denies dysuria, urethral discharge, fever, or prior trauma. Vital signs are: temperature 37.1 C, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, heart rate 112/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. Physical examination reveals an exquisitely tender, edematous, erythematous left hemiscrotum. The left testis is swollen, high-riding, and oriented in a horizontal (transverse) lie. Light stroking of the left inner thigh fails to elicit ipsilateral testicular elevation (absent cremasteric reflex). The right hemiscrotum and right testis are normal. Urinalysis reveals clear yellow urine with no leukocytes, nitrites, or erythrocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the clinical management of this patient?

options.text: Perform emergent duplex Doppler scrotal ultrasonography and delay surgical consultation until radiological confirmation
options.explanation: When clinical features are classic in a surgical window (2 hours), delaying operative exploration for an ultrasound risks testicular ischemia and necrosis.

options.text: Prescribe oral ceftriaxone and doxycycline for acute epididymo-orchitis and discharge with scrotal support
options.explanation: Epididymo-orchitis typically has a subacute onset, positive Prehn sign, normal cremasteric reflex, pyuria on urinalysis, and dysuria; misdiagnosing torsion as epididymitis leads to testicular loss.

options.text: Immediate transfer to the operating room for emergency surgical scrotal exploration, detorsion, and bilateral orchiopexy
options.explanation: This patient presents with acute testicular torsion, a surgical emergency caused by twisting of the spermatic cord, compromising venous outflow followed by arterial inflow, resulting in testicular ischemia and infarction. It occurs most commonly in adolescents due to a congenital anatomical variant called the "bell-clapper deformity" (failure of normal posterior anchoring of the testis and epididymis to the tunica vaginalis, allowing the testis to twist freely on its vascular pedicle). Cardinal diagnostic features include: sudden severe scrotal pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding testis with horizontal lie, and ABSENCE of the cremasteric reflex (the most sensitive physical exam finding, sensitivity > 99%). Testicular salvage is strictly time-dependent: salvage rates exceed 90% if detorsion occurs within 6 hours of symptom onset, but drop to < 10% after 24 hours. When clinical suspicion is high (severe acute onset, absent cremasteric reflex, horizontal lie in a teenager), IMMEDIATE emergency scrotal exploration without delay is mandatory. While Doppler ultrasound can demonstrate absent intratesticular blood flow, imaging must NEVER delay operative exploration if ultrasound cannot be performed immediately. During surgery, the affected testis is untwisted; if viable, it is fixed to the scrotal wall (orchiopexy). Crucially, BILATERAL orchiopexy is mandatory because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral in the vast majority of patients, placing the contralateral testis at extreme risk of future torsion.

options.text: Attempt bedside manual detorsion ("opening a book" technique) and discharge if pain resolves completely
options.explanation: Manual detorsion may be attempted while preparing the operating room, but it never substitutes for surgery because partial torsion or reperfusion failure can persist; surgical exploration and bilateral orchiopexy are mandatory.

options.text: Administer intravenous ketorolac and observe in the emergency department for 4 hours to assess for spontaneous detorsion
options.explanation: Observation allows irreversible ischemic necrosis of germ cells and Sertoli cells; delay beyond 6 hours results in permanent orchiectomy.

explanation: Testicular torsion (sudden pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex) is a surgical emergency with a 6-hour salvage window. Immediate scrotal exploration with detorsion and BILATERAL orchiopexy is mandatory. Bilateral fixation is required because the underlying anatomical defect ("bell-clapper deformity") is bilateral. Operative exploration must not be delayed for ultrasound if high clinical suspicion exists.
objective: Prioritize emergent surgical exploration and bilateral orchiopexy for acute testicular torsion within the 6-hour window and avoid diagnostic delays.
keyPoints: Testicular torsion hallmarks: acute severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex.
Salvage window is < 6 hours; do not delay surgical intervention for ultrasound.
Surgical exploration mandates BILATERAL orchiopexy due to the bilateral nature of bell-clapper anomaly.

subject: Medicine
topic: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN: Drug Discontinuation & Burn ICU Care
stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of high fever, malaise, sore throat, and a rapidly progressive painful body rash. He was diagnosed with focal epilepsy 3 weeks ago and started on oral lamotrigine. Vital signs are: temperature 39.2 C (102.6 F), blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, heart rate 118/min, and respiratory rate 22/min. Physical examination reveals extensive purpuric macules and targetoid lesions with dusky, necrotic centers covering his face, trunk, and proximal extremities. Flaccid bullae are present, and light lateral pressure on non-blistered erythematous skin results in epidermal sloughing (positive Nikolsky sign). Denuded, weeping skin involves approximately 22% of total body surface area (TBSA). Severe erosions and ulcerations with hemorrhagic crusting involve the lips, oral mucosa, and conjunctivae bilaterally. Complete blood count shows marked lymphopenia with normal platelets and no eosinophilia. Which of the following is the most critical initial step in the clinical management of this patient?

options.text: Continue lamotrigine at a reduced dose while administering oral diphenhydramine and topical hydrocortisone
options.explanation: Continuing the culprit drug in SJS/TEN drastically accelerates epidermal necrolysis and is lethal; the offending drug must be stopped immediately.

options.text: Perform aggressive surgical sharp debridement of all involved denuded epidermis in the operating room
options.explanation: Unlike necrotizing fasciitis or deep burns, SJS/TEN involves epidermal cleavage at the dermo-epidermal junction; aggressive surgical debridement strips viable dermis and increases mortality.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous vancomycin and clindamycin for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)
options.explanation: SSSS occurs in neonates and young children due to exfoliative toxin targeting desmoglein-1, spares mucosal membranes, and does not cause targetoid lesions or extensive visceral involvement.

options.text: Immediately discontinue lamotrigine, calculate the SCORTEN prognostic score, and transfer the patient directly to an intensive care burn unit for aggressive supportive fluid and wound care
options.explanation: This patient presents with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN) overlap, a severe, life-threatening mucocutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by extensive keratinocyte apoptosis and epidermal detachment mediated by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+) and natural killer cells via granulysin and Fas-Fas ligand interactions. It is classified by percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) epidermal detachment: SJS (< 10% TBSA), SJS/TEN overlap (10–30% TBSA, as in this patient with 22%), and TEN (> 30% TBSA). Common culprit drugs include anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin), allopurinol, sulfonamide antibiotics, and NSAIDs, typically manifesting 1–4 weeks after initiation. Cardinal features include high fever, severe painful mucosal erosion (at least 2 mucosal sites: oral, ocular, urogenital), purpuric macules with dusky centers, and flaccid bullae with positive Nikolsky sign. The single most important determinant of survival is IMMEDIATE discontinuation of all potential culprit medications; delayed cessation dramatically increases mortality. Patients must be transferred immediately to an accredited burn center or specialized intensive care unit. Supportive care parallels burn management: meticulous thermoregulation, sterile barrier wound care without surgical debridement, fluid resuscitation to replace insensible losses, nutritional support, and aggressive ophthalmologic consultation to prevent permanent cicatricial blindness. SCORTEN is calculated within 24 hours to predict mortality.

options.text: Prescribe oral valacyclovir for suspected disseminated herpes simplex virus infection
options.explanation: Targetoid lesions of erythema multiforme minor from HSV do not cause extensive flaccid bullae, > 20% TBSA epidermal detachment, or systemic toxicity.

explanation: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN overlap (10-30% BSA epidermal sloughing, positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement) is a dermatological emergency most commonly caused by anticonvulsants (lamotrigine), allopurinol, or sulfonamides. The single most critical step is IMMEDIATE discontinuation of the culprit drug, followed by SCORTEN calculation and transfer to a burn intensive care unit for fluid resuscitation and sterile supportive wound care. Aggressive surgical debridement is harmful.
objective: Prioritize immediate culprit drug cessation and transfer to a specialized burn unit for SJS/TEN overlap while avoiding surgical debridement.
keyPoints: SJS/TEN: mucosal involvement (>= 2 sites), positive Nikolsky sign, full-thickness epidermal necrosis.
SJS (< 10% BSA), SJS/TEN overlap (10–30% BSA), TEN (> 30% BSA).
Immediate culprit drug cessation and burn ICU transfer are the primary determinants of survival.

subject: Ethics
topic: Medical Error Disclosure & Transparent Physician Communication Protocol
stem: A 62-year-old woman is hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia. Her physician writes an order for intravenous levofloxacin 750 mg daily. Due to a transcription error by the pharmacy technician and a nurse failing to perform standard two-patient-identifier barcode scanning, the patient inadvertently receives an intravenous dose of 150 mg of succinylcholine intended for a patient in the adjacent room undergoing emergency intubation. Within minutes, the patient developed complete flaccid muscular paralysis and acute respiratory arrest. The rapid response team was immediately activated, and the patient was emergently endotracheally intubated and mechanically ventilated. Four hours later, the paralytic effect has fully dissipated, the patient is successfully extubated, and she is fully alert, oriented, and neurologically intact without permanent physiological harm. The patient asks the attending physician, "Why did I stop breathing and end up with a breathing tube down my throat?" Which of the following is the most ethically and legally appropriate response by the attending physician?

options.text: Inform the patient that she experienced an unpredictable idiosyncratic adverse allergic reaction to levofloxacin requiring temporary intubation
options.explanation: Lying to or misleading a patient violates the core ethical principles of veracity, beneficence, and autonomy, and severely breaches professional ethics.

options.text: Disclose that an error occurred but explicitly state that the nursing and pharmacy departments were solely at fault
options.explanation: Deflecting blame onto other healthcare colleagues undermines multidisciplinary teamwork and patient trust; systemic errors must be addressed professionally and institutionally.

options.text: Withhold disclosure of the medication administration error because the paralysis was transient and the patient suffered no permanent physiological disability
options.explanation: Physicians have an ethical mandate to disclose medical errors that alter patient care or require invasive rescue, even if no permanent physical harm occurs.

options.text: Advise the patient to consult the hospital risk management and legal department before answering any medical questions
options.explanation: Deflecting communication to risk management abandons the physician's clinical and ethical duty to provide transparent medical care to the patient.

options.text: Provide a full, transparent disclosure of the medication error, explain the clinical consequences and corrective actions taken, offer an honest apology, and outline the systemic steps being implemented to prevent recurrence
options.explanation: Ethical codes from the American Medical Association (AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 8.1), the Joint Commission, and hospital quality safety standards require full, transparent, and prompt disclosure of all medical errors that cause harm or meaningful clinical consequence to patients. The obligation to disclose is rooted in the ethical principle of patient AUTONOMY and truthful communication (veracity), which fosters trust in the physician-patient relationship. Professional standards mandate: (1) Prompt in-person disclosure by the attending physician, (2) Direct, objective explanation of exactly what occurred and why without obfuscation or medical jargon, (3) Detailed explanation of the consequences and the treatments administered to reverse the error, (4) An empathetic, sincere apology expressing regret for the event, and (5) Description of the institutional quality improvement process and systemic safety measures implemented to ensure the error does not happen to other patients. Withholding the disclosure because "no permanent harm occurred" or deflecting personal responsibility onto the nurse or pharmacy is unethical and violates national patient safety standards.

explanation: Physicians have an ethical obligation (AMA Code of Ethics) to provide full, honest, and prompt disclosure of medical errors that result in harm or altered clinical status, regardless of whether permanent disability occurred. Disclosure requires explaining what happened, how it was managed, apologizing for the harm, and detailing systemic steps taken to prevent recurrence. Withholding disclosure or deflecting blame onto others is unethical.
objective: Apply the ethical principles of autonomy and veracity to execute transparent medical error disclosure, apology, and systemic remediation.
keyPoints: Full, prompt, transparent disclosure of medical errors is ethically mandatory.
Disclosure includes: facts of the error, consequences/remediation, sincere apology, and systemic prevention.
Absence of permanent harm does NOT excuse non-disclosure; lying or deflecting blame is unethical.
